notes.meaning: All the tribes of Israel met with David at Hebron to make him king. They reminded him that they were his own flesh and blood, meaning they were united as one family with a common heritage.

The people recognised that David had already led them into battle successfully even while Saul was still reigning. More importantly, they remembered God's promise that David would care for Israel like a shepherd and lead them as their ruler.

The elders of Israel gathered before David to establish an agreement between the king and the people under God's guidance. They then anointed him king, fulfilling the promise God had spoken through the prophet Samuel years before.
David marched with the army to Jerusalem, which was then called Jebus. The city was still held by the Jebusites, a local Canaanite people who had lived there for generations.

The Jebusites mocked David and boasted that he would never be able to enter their fortress. David proved them wrong by breaking through their defenses and capturing the hill of Zion, which became known as the City of David.
David offered the highest military post to the soldier brave enough to strike the enemy first. Joab rose to the challenge, led the attack, and earned his place as commander of the army.
David made the captured stronghold his new home and center of power. Because he lived and ruled there, people began calling the fortress the City of David.

David expanded and fortified the surrounding city, building walls from the supporting terraces inward. Meanwhile, Joab took charge of rebuilding the older parts of town that had been damaged in the fighting.
David's power, influence, and honor grew steadily over time. His real strength came not from his own skill, but because the Lord of hosts was watching over and helping him.
A record is given of David's bravest fighters who stood firmly with him and the nation. These men used their strength to help establish his kingdom in keeping with God's word.
Jashobeam stood as the leader of the top officers. He performed an astonishing feat in battle by fighting with his spear and killing three hundred enemies in a single fight.
Eleazar, the son of Dodo, was second in rank among David's top three elite champions. He became famous for his loyalty and extraordinary bravery on the battlefield.

At Pas-dammim, the Philistines attacked while the Israelite army fled in panic across a field ripe with barley. Eleazar and David stood their ground in the middle of the field, fought off the enemy, and the Lord gave them a great victory.
Three leading officers from the Thirty came down to join David at his rocky hideout in the cave of Adullam. Meanwhile, a Philistine raiding party was camped in the nearby Valley of Rephaim.
David remained inside his mountain fortress while enemy Philistine soldiers occupied his hometown of Bethlehem. An enemy guard post controlled the town and its entrance.
Thirsty and worn out, David voiced a sudden, deep craving for a drink of fresh water from the well by the gate of Bethlehem. He was fondly remembering the sweet water of the town where he grew up.
Out of sheer devotion to David, the three warriors slipped past enemy lines, drew the water, and brought it back. Instead of drinking it, David poured it onto the ground as an offering to God.

David declared he could not drink water that had cost men the risk of their lives, treating it as if it were their very blood. Because their sacrifice was so costly, he felt only God was worthy to receive it.
Abishai, the brother of Joab, was the leader of the second group of three warriors. He earned great renown by taking up his spear against three hundred enemy soldiers and killing them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think verses 20-25 come from a separate source. They suggest parts may be quoted from a lost poem praising Abishai and Benaiah.

notes.meaning: Abishai was held in higher esteem than the other men in his group and served as their commander. Even so, he did not reach the elite status of the first three champions.

notes.meaning: Benaiah was a fearless fighter from southern Judah who performed many daring deeds. He defeated two mighty Moabite champions, and on a freezing day he climbed into a pit to fight and kill a lion.

Benaiah also faced an Egyptian giant who stood about seven and a half feet tall and carried a massive spear. Armed with only a wooden staff, Benaiah grabbed the giant's weapon and killed him with his own spear.
These bold actions made Benaiah famous throughout the land. His bravery earned him an honored name alongside the three mighty warriors of the second rank.
